1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE*
 Amicus Renée Lettow Lerner  is the Donald
Phillip Rothschild Research  Professor of Law at the
George Washington University Law  School. She is a
legal historian specializing in the history of the jury
in England and the United States. Her interest in this
case is to assist the Court in understanding the original practice of the jury.


* University affiliation of amicus curiae is provided for identification purposes only. Pursuant to this Court’s Rule 37.6, amicus
curiae states that this brief was not authored in whole or in part
by counsel for any party, and that no person or entity other than
amicus curiae monetarily contributed to the preparation or submission of this brief.

2
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
 At the time of the ratification of the Sixth
Amendment, in the late eighteenth century in England and the United States, jury trial was the exclusive means of resolving felony cases.  Plea bargaining
and bench trials were unknown.  English and American judges understood that jury trial needed to be efficient and that requiring twelve lay jurors to be
unanimous presents considerable challenges.  Possible difficulties include lengthy trials and deliberations as well as hung juries, with the expensive and
time-consuming remedy of trying the case again to a
different jury. Because of these problems, in the late
eighteenth century the English and American legal
systems had rules and practices that were designed to
speed jury trial and to further unanimity of twelve jurors in a reasonable time.
 These practices included judges commenting
on evidence to the jury, use of experienced jurors and
foremen, juror deprivation and sequestration, and
limited or no voir dire.  The procedures were considered important, and in some instances vital, to a functioning jury system. English and American judges understood that without such practices, jury trial would
become too lengthy to be workable in many cases.  As
these practices faded over time, so did jury trial.
 Today, the overwhelming majority of  criminal
cases are resolved not by jury trial but by plea bargain. Without these historical practices, or suitable
alternatives, the effect of mandating twelve unanimous jurors would ironically be that fewer jury trials

3
will be held.  Prosecutors will have even stronger incentives to offer plea deals that will be difficult for defendants to refuse.  Isolated features of the eighteenth-century trial by jury would be preserved, at the
expense of actual criminal jury trials.  It is not
originalism, but eclecticism, to insist on twelve jurors
in criminal cases without the supporting common-law
practices that made that number workable.
ARGUMENT
I. The late eighteenth-century legal systems
in England and America had rules and
practices, no longer in effect, that were designed to encourage efficient deliberations.
 It is difficult to get twelve persons to agree
unanimously on almost anything, much less a serious
criminal charge.  In the common -law system, courts
and legislatures worked together to develop a set of
rules that encouraged twelve jurors to reach unanimity in a reasonable time. These rules and practices included external assistance—the judge commenting on
evidence to the jury; internal assistance —the presence of an experienced foreman and other experienced
jurors; and time pressure —deprivation and sequestration.
A. Judges regularly commented on evidence
to the jury.
 In the eighteenth- century English and American legal systems, a major contributor to twelve jurors
being able to achieve unanimity efficiently was the
widespread practice of trial judges summing up and
commenting on the evidence.  The practice was the

4
same in criminal and civil cases. Jurors were not left
to puzzle over lengthy and nearly incomprehensible
instructions on law with no help on the facts, as they
so often are today. At common law, in many cases the
judge guided the jury on the facts, and the jury usually followed that guidance.  In effect, there was a
partnership between the judge and the jury in deciding the case, not the rigid formal separation existing
today.
 When the common- law tradition of judicial
comment eroded in the United States during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, prominent American
scholars of evidence such as James Bradley Thayer
and John H. Wigmore were deeply concerned. Thayer
wrote that it is
impossible to conceive of trial by jury as
existing [in England] in a form which
would withhold from the jury the assistance of the Court in dealing with the
facts. Trial by jury, in such a form as
that, is not a trial by jury in any historical sense of the words.  It is not the venerated institution which attracted the
praise of Blackstone and of our ancestors, but something novel, modern, and
much less to be respected.
James B. Thayer, A Preliminary Treatise on Evidence
at the Common Law  188 n.2 (1898) . For Wigmore,
“this unfortunate [American] departure from the orthodox common law rule has done more than any
other one thing to impair the general efficiency of jury
trial as an instrument of justice.” 9 John H. Wigmore,

5
A Treatise on the Anglo-American System of Evidence
in Trials at Common Law  § 2551, at 504–505 (3d ed.
1940). Thayer and Wigmore recognized the crucial
role of the judge in helping to guide twelve jurors to
unanimity.
 At common law in England, a judge’s charge to
the jury did not separate instructions on law from
comments on evidence; the judge folded them together. Thomas A. Green, Verdict According to Conscience 139 (1985). The judge endeavored to help the
jurors sort out the facts, particularly in cases of conflicting testimony.  Matthew Hale (1609- 1676), who
served as a judge of all three superior common -law
courts, including as Chief Justice of the Court of
King’s Bench, which decided felony cases, wrote of the
“Excellency” of the practice of judges commenting on
evidence. The trial judge was not only able to “direct”
the jurors on questions of law, but also
in Matters of Fact, to give them a great
Light and Assistance by his weighing
the Evidence before them, and observing
where the Question and Knot of the
Business lies, and by showing them his
Opinion even in Matter of Fact, which is
a great Advantage and L ight to Lay
Men.
Matthew Hale, The History of the Common Law of
England 164–165 (Charles M. Gray ed., 1971) (1713)
(Hale, History of the Common Law).
 In the mid-eighteenth century, Blackstone also
praised judicial comment on evidence.  He described,

6
at the end of a trial, the judge summing up the evidence for the jury and “observing wherein the main
question and principal issue lies, stating what evidence has been given to support it, with the remarks
as to the credibility of the witnesses, and how far they
have been contradicted or supported by others.” 3 William Blackstone, Commentaries *375. Blackstone emphasized the benefits of the practice. “This having the
judge’s observation upon the evidence, is a most advantageous usage of the English law. For the jury are
usually unpracticed in such matters, and are liable to
be misled by the eloquence of counsel, or their own
lack of experience.” Id.
 Judicial comment on evidence continued vigorously on both sides of the Atlantic through the eighteenth century, and juries mostly followed the judges’
lead. In 1773, James Boswell asked Lord Mansfield,
the Chief Justice of King’s Bench, whether juries always followed his recommendations.  Mansfield replied that juries did, “except in political causes.”  1
James Oldham, The Mansfield Manuscripts and the
Growth of English Law in the Eighteenth Century 206
n.44 (1992) (Oldham, Mansfield) (quoting 7 The Private Papers of James Boswell from Malahide Castle
109 (G. Scott & F.A. Pottle eds., 1928)); see also John
H. Langbein, Blackstone on Judging , in Blackstone
and His Commentaries: Biography, Law, History  65,
70–71 & nn.33–35 (Wilfrid Prest ed., 2009)  (discussing judges routinely guiding juries in both civil and
criminal cases). Sometimes a judge strongly indicated
the verdict he favored; sometimes he contented himself with a broad hint.  See John H. Langbein, The

7
Criminal Trial Before the Lawyers, 45 U. Chi. L. Rev.
263, 286 (1978)  (Langbein, Criminal Trial) . Juries
were not legally obligated to follow a judge’s views,
but they ordinarily did. Oldham, Mansfield, supra, at
150.
 Over time, the character of judicial comment
changed somewhat, as trials increasingly featured
lawyers. By the late eighteenth century in criminal
cases, judges more rarely stated their opinions about
the outcome plainly. But they continued to comment
on evidence and gave more detailed summaries of the
evidence, guiding the juries to the important points.
See John H. Langbein, The Origins of Adversary
Criminal Trial 322–323 (2003); Renée Lettow Lerner,
How the Creation of Appellate Courts in England and
the United States Limited Judicial Comment on Evidence to the Jury , 40 J. Legal Prof. 215, 229 –230
(2016) (Lerner, Appellate Courts). The implication is
that the advent of counsel, especially defense counsel,
tended to obscure the crucial questions of fact.
 Many judges in the United States availed
themselves of their common -law powers to comment
on evidence. Federal judges, with the security and authority of life tenure, were known for robust comment.
In 1886, the U.S. Supreme Court gave a resounding
endorsement of the practice:
In the courts of the United States, as in
those of England, from which our practice was derived, the judge, in submitting a case to the jury, may, at his discretion, whenever he thinks it necessary

8
to assist them in arriving at a just conclusion, comment upon the evidence, call
their attention to parts of it which he
thinks important, and express his opinion upon the facts; and the expression of
such an opinion, when no rule of law is
incorrectly stated, and all matters of fact
are ultimately submitted to the determination of the jury, cannot be reviewed on
writ of error.
Vicksburg & Meridian R.R. Co. v. Putnam , 118 U.S.
545, 553 (1886).
 In 1887, and in several cases thereafter, the
Court defined the constitutional phrase “trial by jury”
to mean a trial in which the judge had the power to
comment on the evidence.  United States v. Philadelphia & Reading R.R. Co. , 123 U.S. 113, 114 (1887)
(“Trial by jury in the courts of the United States is a
trial presided over by a judge, with authority, not only
to rule on objections to evidence, and to instruct the
jury upon the law, but also, when in his judgment the
due administration of justice req uires it, to aid the
jury by explaining and commenting upon the testimony, and even giving them his opinion upon questions of fact  . . . .”); see also  Capitol Traction Co. v.
Hof, 174 U.S. 1, 13–14 (1899) (same); Patton v. United
States, 281 U.S. 276, 289 (1930)  (same). In 1930, the
Court declared that this power, among certain other
attributes of a common-law trial, was “beyond the authority of the legislative department to destroy or
abridge.” Patton, 281 U.S. at  290. This Court made
clear that the judge’s power to comment on evidence

9
was a crucial element of trial by jury under the U.S.
Constitution.
 State appellate courts also encouraged trial
judges to exercise their powers to comment.  For example, in 1830 in Massachusetts, Chief Justice Isaac
Parker rejected an argument that a trial judge had
improperly commented on evidence in a criminal libel
case. “We know of no rule requiring the judge to conceal his opinion. He is to comment upon the evidence.”
Commonwealth v. Child , 27 Mass. 252, 260  (1830)
(opinion of Parker, C.J.). He asked rhetorically: “Is he
to do it by merely stating that one witness says this
thing and another says that? Has he not power to say,
this evidence is weak and that evidence is strong?” Id.
At that time, appellate judges in Massachusetts also
sat as trial judges. Chief Justice Parker described his
own practice when presiding over trials. When the evidence was nearly balanced, “I endeavor to leave it to
the jury to decide which scale preponderates; but if
the evidence on one side is strong, compared with that
on the other side, I think it my duty to make the jury
comprehend that it is so.” Id.1 Such judicial comment
encouraged twelve jurors to arrive at a unanimous
verdict efficiently.
 In the nineteenth century and into the twentieth, state and federal judges’ power to comment on
evidence eroded. Judicial elections and the increasing

1 For additional examples of state judges exercising the power to
comment in criminal and civil cases, see cases collected in Renée
Lettow Lerner, The Transformation of the American Civil Trial:
The Silent Judge, 42 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 195, 214 & n.70 (2000).

10
separation between trial and appellate courts played
a role. See generally Renée Lettow Lerner, The Transformation of the American Civil Trial: The Silent
Judge, 42 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 195 (2000) (describing
the process of limiting trial judges’ power to comment
on evidence); Lerner, Appellate Courts, supra (same).
The waning of the traditional common -law power in
the United States prompted the troubled comments of
Thayer and Wigmore quoted above.  Both recognized
the importance of judicial comment in guiding the jurors and helping the twelve to agree.
B. Jurors were often experienced, especially
foremen.
 In addition to the guidance of the judge, late
eighteenth-century jurors in England and America often had guidance from other members of the panel
who were repeat players. These repeat jurors tended
to be familiar with the law and courtroom proceedings, a familiarity that helped them to decide cases
quickly. Foremen were often especially experienced
and therefore could guide juries effectively in making
decisions. This practice helped to persuade twelve jurors to be unanimous in a reasonable time.
 In England, the same persons tended to be
called for jury service again and again. 2 Repeat service occurred often enough that some members of

2 In part, this was because of property qualifications.  In England, the same basic property qualification was in place from the
late seventeenth century until 1972: ownership of freehold land
that produced at least £10 in value a year.  4 W. & M., c. 24
(1692); 3 Geo. 2, c. 25 (1730). (This qualification was repealed in

11
every trial jury in one sample from  the eighteenth
century had served before.  John M. Beattie, Crime
and the Courts in England, 1660-1800, at 386 (1986).
On average, more than a third of jurors on a panel had
served at a previous court session. Id. at 385–386. In
London, most of the dozen jurors impaneled for a
given session of court had served in prior sessions.
Langbein, Criminal Trial, supra, at 276–277. In theory, jurors in England were not supposed to serve
more than one session every two years.  Jury Act of
1730, 3 Geo. 2, c. 25.  But in practice, this rule was
frequently disregarded. See Beattie, supra, at 386.
 Moreover, a juror was likely to hear many cases
in a row once he appeared for a particular court session, which lasted several days.  A juror could decide
dozens of cases during a single session. See James S.
Cockburn, Twelve Silly Men? The Trial Jury at Assizes, 1560-1670, in Twelve Good Men and True 158,
165–166 (James S. Cockburn & Thomas A. Green
eds., 1988) (Twelve Good Men and True); Beattie, supra, at 380–382; Langbein, Criminal Trial, supra, at
274–276. By the middle of the eighteenth century, it
was “entirely typical” for eight men out of the twelve
to hear all of the dozens of cases “tried between Friday

the Criminal Justice Act 1972, c. 71.) The property qualification
meant that juries largely consisted of yeoman farmers in rural
areas and merchants in cities. See P.J.R. King, “Illiterate Plebeians, Easily Misled”: Jury Composition, Experience, and Behavior in Essex, 1735-1815, at 254, 261, and Douglas Hay, The Class
Composition of the Palladium of Liberty: Trial Jurors in the
Eighteenth Century, 305, 349, 357, both in Twelve Good Men and
True (James S. Cockburn & Thomas A. Green eds., 1988).

12
afternoon and the following Thursday,” in the English
criminal courts. Beattie, supra, at 382 n.175.
 In England, foremen exercised considerable
leadership, helping the twelve jurors to make decisions rapidly. Beattie, supra, at 397– 398; Cockburn,
Twelve Silly Men , supra, at 158 , 170–171. The position of foreman became almost an office. He was often
a person of higher standing in the community than
the typical juror. Thomas A. Green, A Retrospective on
the Criminal Trial Jury, 1200 -1800, in Twelve Good
Men and True, supra, at 358, 378; Cockburn, Twelve
Silly Men, supra, at 158, 167–171. Above all, foremen
were called to serve repeatedly. For instance, in Kent
in the mid -seventeenth century, one person, Robert
Day, served as a juror in at least 118 trials, 11 1 of
them as foreman, over the course of 13 years.  Cockburn, Twelve Silly Men, supra, at 158, 168.
 Information about eighteenth -century American juries is sparser, but suggests that, as in England,
American courts relied on experienced jurors and
foremen. William E. Nelson, The Legal Restraint of
Power in Pre -Revolutionary America: Massachusetts
As a Case Study, 1760-1775, 18 Am. J. Legal Hist. 1,
13–14 (1974); William E. Nelson, Americanization of
the Common Law  21 (1975). For instance, records
from the federal circuit court in Virginia indicate that
roughly twenty-five percent of jurors served as repeat
members of the grand jury.  Wythe Holt & B rent
Tarter, The Apparent Political Selection of Federal
Grand Juries in Virginia, 1789-1809, 49 Am. J. Legal
Hist. 257, 262– 263 (2007) . One person, William

13
Branch Giles, served as foreman of the federal grand
jury in Virginia three years in a row, from 1803 to
1805. He had been a member of the U.S. House of Representatives and was a U.S. Senator from 1804 to
1815. Id. at 263.
 The prior experience of the jurors had great effect on a jury’s ability to deliberate efficiently.  Experienced foremen and experienced jurors helped guide
the other members of the panel to an efficient decision, a result that would otherwise be difficult with a
group of twelve.
C. Jurors were subject to systematic deprivation and sequestration.
 In the late eighteenth century, another important tool that the English and American legal systems used to achieve unanimity among twelve jurors
was the time pressure of systematic deprivation and
sequestration. (Sequestration was also referred to as
prohibiting separation of the jury.) In the early seventeenth century, Edward Coke gave the classic formulation of the rule:
By the Law of England a Jury after their
Evidence given upon the Issue, ought to
be kept together in some convenient
place, without Meat [food] or Drinke,
Fire or Candle, which some Bookes call
an Imprisonment, and without speech
with any, unlesse it be the Bailife, and
with him onely if they be agreed.
Edward Coke, The First Part of the Institutes of the
Laws of England 471 (1628) (“Of Estates” § 366, folio

14
227b). Coke declared this formulation in the context
of discussing civil cases, but elsewhere he emphasized
the necessity of strict adherence to the rule of juror
confinement in felony cases. Edward Coke, The Third
Part of the Institutes  of the Laws of England  121
(1680) (“Larceny or Theft” ch. 47, folio 110); see also 2
Matthew Hale, History of the Pleas of the Crown 297
(1736) (repeating the rule) (Hale, Pleas of the Crown).
 The rule of deprivation and sequestration of jurors appeared early in English law, and English
judges refined and enforced it through the Middle
Ages and into the eighteenth century. A rule concerning jury deprivation and sequestration appears in the
Fleta treatise in the 1290s. Fleta, Of the Verdict of the
Jurors, in Book III and Book IV, 89 Selden Society 66
(H.G. Richardson & G.O. Sayles trans., 1972). Judges
enforced the rule by imprisoning jurors caught snacking or separating from their fellows (before the eighteenth century), fining jurors, and sometimes rejecting
verdicts. David J. Seipp, Jurors, Evidences and the
Tempest of 1499, in The Dearest Birthright of the People of England: The Jury in the History of the Common
Law 75, 86 –89 (John Cairns & Grant McLeod eds.,
2002); J.H. Baker, Introduction, in The Reports of Sir
John Spelman Part II, 94 Selden Society 83, 112–113
(1978).
 In explaining the existing practice in 1768, William Blackstone declared that the purpose of the rule
was “to avoid intemperance and causeless delay.”  3
William Blackstone, Commentaries *375–376. Commentators on this rule have linked it with the need for

15
the common -law system to encourage speedy jury
unanimity among a jury of twelve.  See, e.g. , Baker,
supra, at 112; Seipp, supra, at 88–89. Another reason
was to prevent parties from treating the jurors or
tampering with them and causing partiality or the appearance of partiality. Baker, supra, at 112; Seipp, supra, at 87–88.
 Blackstone and other eighteenth-century writers suggested that the rule of deprivation had begun
to relax somewhat. Blackstone added an exception to
Coke’s formulation and stated that jurors are to be
kept “without meat, drink, fire, or candle, unless by
permission of the judge, till they are all unanimously
agreed.” 3 William Blackstone, Commentaries *375–
376 (emphasis added). By the eighteenth century, the
question of allowing the jurors refreshment was thus
left to the discretion of the judge.  Judges routinely
made exceptions for jurors who were ill.  See 2 Hale,
Pleas of the Crown, supra, at 297 n.(c); The Complete
Juryman 169 (1752). Still, in many cases in the eighteenth century the judges did enforce the rule, as repeated references in cases, legal treatises, and the
broader culture indicate.3

3 In a case in 1735, the Court of Common Pleas set out the basic
rule that was followed in England and widely in the American
colonies and United States from the eighteenth through the
early nineteenth century: If the jury separated or ate or drank
at their own expense without the court’s permission, the jurors
were misbehaving and fineable, but the verdict would not be
overturned unless the jury’s impartiality were in doubt. But if a
party treated the jurors to food or drink before the verdict, the
judge would set aside a verdict in that party’s favor.  St. John v.
Abbot, 94 Eng. Rep. 994, 994 (C.P. 1735). For descriptions of the

16
 Along with many other English practices concerning juries, the rule of juror deprivation and sequestration crossed the Atlantic to the North American colonies. For example, a Virginia statute of 1645
provided that jurors were “to be kept from food and
releife till they have agreed upon their verdict according to the custome practised in England.”  Act 10, 20
Car. 1 (1645), in 1 William Waller Hening, The Statutes at Large: Being a Collection of All the Laws of
Virginia, from the First Session of the Legislature, in
the Year 1619, at 303 (1823); see also Act 37, 14 C ar.
2 (1662) , in 2 Hening, supra, at 74 (“[W]hen ever a
jury is sent out, an officer sworn to that purpose shall
keep them from meat and drink untill [sic] they have
agreed on their verdict.”) . A Connecticut statute in
force in 1702 declared: “And when the court have committed any case to the consideration of the jury, the
jury shall be confined, under custody of an officer appointed by the court until they are agreed on a verdict.” Conn. Gen. Stat. , tit. 6, c. 1, §  11. Two federal

rule in treatises, see, e.g., The Complete Juryman, supra, at 158–
159, 168–173; Hale, History of the Common Law , supra, at 165;
1 Giles Duncomb, Trials per Pais 247–249 (8th ed. 1766); 5 John
Comyns & Stewart Kyd,  A Digest of the Laws of England  535–
537 (4th ed. 1793) (“Pleader,” §§ 44–46). For references in wider
culture, see Charles Clay Doyle & Clement Charles Doyle,
“Wretches Hang That Jury-men May Dine,” 28 Just. Sys. J. 219,
220 (2007) (commenting on a couplet in Alexander Pope’s 1714
mock epic The Rape of the Lock ); Thomas Rowlandson, “A Lamentable Case of a Jury -Man” (1815) (etching satirizing the confinement of jurors without necessities), reprinted in  John H.
Langbein, Renée Lettow Lerner & Bruce P. Smith, History of the
Common Law: The Development of Anglo -American Legal Institutions 420 (2009).

17
court opinions quoted or cited this statute as remaining in force in 1808 and 1809. See Lester v. Stanley, 15
F. Cas. 396, 396– 397 & n.2 (C.C.D. Conn. 1808) (No.
8,277) (setting aside verdict because the jury separated before agreeing on the verdict); see also Howard
v. Cobb, 12 F. Cas. 636, 636 (C.C.D. Conn. 1809) (No.
6,755) (“[J]udgement must have been arrested if it
had been proved that the jury separated before they
had agreed upon a verdict .” (citing Conn. Gen. Stat.,
tit. 6, c. 1, §  11)). Both of these federal opinions suggest that state judges in Connecticut sometimes allowed juries to separate before agreeing on a verdict.
 Generally, the sequestration of jurors did not
present a problem in the eighteenth century, because
trials almost never lasted longer than a day. A notable
exception was the Boston Massacre trials in 1770.
Several of those trials lasted about a week. The jurors
in each case were kept together and confined to the
courthouse or to the jail er’s house under keepers for
the entire period of the trial, to conform with the sequestration rules. 3 John Adams, The Legal Papers of
John Adams 19, 21 (L. Kinvin Wroth & Hiller B. Zobel
eds., 1965) (quoting early accounts); Hiller B. Zobel,
The Boston Massacre 225, 250, 273–274 (1970).
 In the debates over the ratification of the U.S.
Constitution, ratification supporter John Dickinson
referred to the rules of jury deprivation and sequestration. Responding to the Anti-Federalists’ objection
to the lack of a right to civil jury trial, Dickinson jokingly argued that the Anti-Federalists were such lovers of liberty that they would never have allowed jury

18
trial to develop  in the first place , as the system  depended on coercion. “What! Can freedom be preserved
by imprisoning its guardians? Can freedom be preserved, by keeping twelve men closely confined without meat, drink, fire, or candle, until they unanimously agree . . . ?” “Fabius” (John Dickinson), Letter
IV: Observations on the Constitution  (Apr. 19, 1788),
reprinted in 17 The Documentary History of the Ratification of the Constitution 180, 183 (John P. Kaminski & Gaspare J. Saladino eds., 1995).
 In the early nineteenth century, the rules
about deprivation and sequestration relaxed on both
sides of the Atlantic.  In 1819, the Court of King’s
Bench declared that judges could permit  the jury to
separate before the verdict  in misdemeanor  cases.
King v. Kinnear, 106 Eng. Rep. 434, 435– 436 (K.B.
1819); see also Marcy Strauss, Sequestration, 24 Am.
J. Crim. L. 63, 71–72 (1996) (describing the later history of sequestration) . Some American states maintained the rigor of the traditional rule, particularly
regarding separation of the jury in a capital case. See,
e.g., Commonwealth v. M’Caul , 3 Va. 271, 301– 306
(1812); McClain v. State, 18 Tenn. 241, 241– 243
(1837); Hare v. State, 5 Miss. 187, 195–196 (1839). But
English and American judges increasingly permitted
jurors to take refreshment and to separate before returning a verdict.  See, e.g. , Commonwealth v. Purchase, 19 Mass. 521, 525  (1824); Commonwealth v.
Clue, 3 Rawle 498, 503 (Pa. 1831).

19
 The relaxation of the ancient rule created a
new problem: the hung jury. In 1867, an English commentator pointed out that juries being supplied with
refreshments but required to be unanimous had led to
difficulty with getting twelve persons to agree expeditiously. He observed that the “modern custom seems
to be for the judge to discharge the jury” so the case
could be tried again to a new jury.  George Overend,
The Preservation and Amendment of Trial by Jury, 23
Law Mag. & L. Rev. Q .J. Juris. 191, 200 (1867) . In
1870, an act of Parliament formally ratified the practice of the jury being allowed refreshment.  Act of
1870, 33 & 34 Vict . c. 77 . Somewhat earlier, some
American states likewise began the practice of discharging a jury which could not agree and ordering a
new trial. See, e.g., Purchase, 19 Mass. at 525; Johnson v. Root , 13 F. Cas. 7 98, 806 –807 (C.C.D. Mass.
1862) (No. 7,409) (hearing the case after a retrial; a
jury disagreed after the first trial and a new trial was
ordered). New trials were an expensive and time-consuming remedy; the system of jury trials became evermore cumbersome. Removing the rules of deprivation
and sequestration provoked difficulties in getting
twelve jurors to agree, a problem which was hard to
solve.
II. Jury selection was swift, with limited or no
voir dire, which allowed rapid empanelment of twelve jurors and efficient jury
trial.
 Besides providing mechanisms to persuade
twelve jurors to agree on a verdict in a timely manner,
the common law streamlined the trial itself.  This

20
streamlining took many forms, but one of the most notable, from a modern perspective, directly bears on
the number of jurors. In criminal cases, jury selection
was very swift. In modern practice, with its extended
voir dire, requiring a greater number of jurors lengthens the process even more.  In contrast, eighteenthcentury practice encouraged impaneling twelve jurors
quickly. This rapidity helped to make jury trials workable as a routine matter.
 In late  eighteenth-century England and the
United States, as in England today, jury selection was
strictly limited.  Voir dire was swift or non -existent.
The defendant or counsel could ask questions directly
related to for -cause challenges, such as whether the
juror met the property qualifications.  John H. Langbein, Renée Lettow Lerner & Bruce P. Smith, History
of the Common Law: The Development of Anglo-American Legal Institutions 540 (2009) . But in the late
eighteenth century, few did so.  Langbein, Criminal
Trial, supra, at 275–276. Further, neither side could
ask a potential juror whether he had prejudged the
case or about other issues of prejudice. Langbein, Lerner & Smith, supra, at 540; April J. Anderson,  Peremptory Challenges at the Turn of the Nineteenth Century, 16 Stan. J.C.R. & C.L. 1, 12–13, 17–18 (2020).
This restriction drastically limited the scope of questioning; it speeded jury selection and helped to prevent exhausting the pool of available jurors.  See The
Trial of Peter Cook, Y.B. 8 Will. 3 (1696), reprinted in
13 How. St. Tr. 311, 334 (1812) (establishing the rule).
For American examples, see State v. Baldwin , 1
Tread. 289, 292 (S.C. 1813); id. at 296–301 (opinion of

21
Nott, J.); id. at 321–325 (opinion of Bay, J.) ; State v.
Flower, 1 Miss. 318, 318 –319 (1829); King v. State, 6
Miss. 730, 734 (1841); State v. Creasman, 32 N.C. 395,
397 (1849); Crippen v. People, 8 Mich. 117, 126 (1860).
 The English legal system maintained the policy
of discouraging extended voir dire; the American system diverged dramatically, allowing ever -more detailed and intrusive questioning that lengthened jury
trial. Two cases, in particular, launched this change:
the trial of James Callender for seditious libel in 1800,
United States v. Callender, 25 F. Cas. 239, 244 (C.C.D.
Va. 1800) (No. 14,709), presided over by Justice Samuel Chase, and the trial of Aaron Burr for treason in
1807, United States v. Burr, 25 F. Cas. 49, 77 (C.C.D.
Va. 1807) (No. 14,692g), presided over by Chief Justice John Marshall. Both these cases were politically
charged and notorious.  At the time, U.S. marshals,
who were responsible for summoning jurors in federal
courts, were suspected of packing juries with political
supporters. See, e.g., Carl E. Prince, Federalists and
the Origins of the U.S. Civil Service 264 (1977); James
Morton Smith, Freedom’s Fetters: The Alien and Sedition Laws and American Civil Liberties  235–236
(1956); Peter Charles Hoffer, The Treason Trials of
Aaron Burr: Landmark Law Cases and American Society 129–132, 146–147 (2008); R. Kent Newmyer, The
Treason Trial of Aaron Burr: Law, Politics, and the
Character Wars of the New Nation 91–94 (2012). Justice Chase and Chief Justice Marshall understandably believed it was necessary for a fair trial (or at least
the appearance of it) to allow the defendant and his
counsel to question the jurors more extensively than

22
had been previously allowed.  But in doing so, they
opened the floodgates. American lawyers seized upon
this opportunity to question jurors and stretched it
immensely, in both criminal and civil cases.
 In extending voir dire, lawyers and judges
helped to destroy the efficiency of jury trial. As a treatise writer in 1877 declared, voir dire has been
“lengthened to a tedious and exasperating extent in
trials of great importance . . . .” John Proffatt, A Treatise on Trial by Jury 220 (1877). Today, this lengthening has occurred in trials of all kinds. Elaborate modern jury selection is far removed from the streamlined
eighteenth-century practice. The more jurors need to
be selected, the longer modern jury selection takes.
And the less the legal system relies on jury trials to
resolve criminal cases.
III. Mandating rigid rules for jury trials can result in more plea bargains, often meaning
no adjudication of any kind.
 The Court’s efforts to further or to preserve
jury trial have sometimes backfired. A notable example is requiring the states to provide jury trial under
the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments  for misdemeanor charges carrying the potential for more than
six months’ imprisonment. Duncan v. Louisiana, 391
U.S. 145, 149–150, 159 (1968). Duncan has not led to
many jury trials in misdemeanor cases.  Rather, the
vast majority of misdemeanor charges are resolved by
plea bargains.
 Flexibility and experimentation are key to
making jury trials workable, meaning reasonable in

23
cost and length.  If jury trials are not efficient, they
will only be held in a very few cases. The legal system
will develop and permit workarounds. The chief workaround, plea bargaining, effectively involves no adjudication at all. A federal judge has to certify that there
is a “factual basis” for the plea, F ed. R. Crim. P.
11(b)(3), but that is a weak and highly variable standard. In the United States, defendants are routinely
sentenced to years of imprisonment without a formal
determination by a jury or a judge that the person is
in fact guilty. A decision to require twelve jurors will
promote further punishment without adjudication.
 A principled originalism does not pluck out one
or two features of a complex common -law institution
such as the jury and impose them on the states.  It is
essential to consider the broader procedural context
of that institution and how it operated historically.
Without that deeper consideration, efforts to preserve
the jury will backfire.
CONCLUSION
 The Court should affirm the judgment of the
Fourth District Court of Appeal of Florida.
